name: Optative if only
pattern: standalone if only + finite clause, often modally remote

entry.name: Optative if only
entry.pattern: standalone if only + finite clause, often modally remote

1.definition: Expresses a wish concerning a possibility or unrealized state.

examples.form: [If only we had brought a torch!]

relatedConstructions.notes: Only if imposes a condition, while if only can express a wish.

projection.target: A consequence can remain unexpressed, and the utterance conveys a wish. In We can enter only if we bring a torch, only if instead sets a necessary condition.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: If only
curious.summary: If only, standing alone, expresses a wish about something that isn't the case or might not be.
curious.body: If only we had brought a torch! is a wish. A result can be left unsaid, and the sentence still conveys the wish. If only is different from only if. We can enter only if we bring a torch sets a necessary condition. If only expresses a wish, and the clause that follows is often remote in its wording.

examples.text: [If only we had brought a torch!]
We can enter only if we bring a torch.

curious.try: Think of something you wish had gone differently. Start the sentence with If only.

teacher.summary: Teaches learners to express a wish with if only, and to tell it from only if.
teacher.explain: Optative if only stands alone with a finite clause, often modally remote: If only we had brought a torch! It expresses a wish concerning a possibility or unrealized state. A consequence can remain unexpressed, and the utterance conveys a wish. Only if instead sets a necessary condition, as in We can enter only if we bring a torch. This dictionary relates the pattern to ordinary if-conditionals and marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Optative is this dictionary’s term for the wish use.

examples.text: [If only we had brought a torch!]
We can enter only if we bring a torch.

contrasts.text: If only we had brought a torch!
We can enter only if we bring a torch.

watch_for: A learner might treat if only as the same as only if, when if only expresses a wish and only if imposes a condition.
A learner might look for a main clause after if only, when the consequence can remain unexpressed.
teacher.activity: Give students situations where something went wrong. They write a wish with If only and a related condition with only if, and say how the two differ.

child.hook: How do you say what you wish had happened?
child.explain: If only can show a wish. If only we had brought a torch! means we wish we had one. It's a wish, so no other part is needed.

examples.text: [If only we had brought a torch!]

child.play: Think of a wish about something that didn't happen. Begin with If only and say it with feeling.
